name: OS-eDRAM: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain-cell memory IP on a U.S. 200mm foundry
kill_reason: Scored 48.0/100 default (rank 36/40), 51.7 moonshot. Weakest: time to revenue 1/5 (48 months (36-60): 18-24 mo module development plus 12-18 mo PBTI/retention qualification before first NRE, past the 36-month hard ceiling.); founder-fit 1/5 (Process-module development and reliability qualification need a device/process CTO and a SkyWater JDA from day one; the founder only adds a ); tech feasibility 2/5 (TRL 4: imec 2T0C cells (IEDM 2020/21) only; PBTI reaches 5-yr at 95C in lab (IEDM 2025 snippet), no 10-yr lifetime, and IWO retention falls ). Scorer verdicts — founder: A $15-40M process-module science project with revenue around 2030 that a pure-CMOS gain cell undercuts; not this founder's venture. | vc: A process-module science project with $15-40M and 48 months to first revenue to win small 130nm royalties, while C-32 serves the same buyer with no new module: pass. | veteran: Real physics on the wrong substrate: no U.S. fab has an oxide module, contamination rules force a dedicated tool set, PBTI is still lab-grade, and a zero-mask Si gain cell serves the same buyer, so it's a 5-year
wins_axis: standby power per bit vs SRAM; ~2-4x on-die density vs 130nm SRAM; write endurance (>1e11) and write energy vs SkyWater-qualified ReRAM for scratchpad/activation memory
buyer: Always-on edge-AI ASICs (keyword spotting, vision wake-up, sensor fusion) and DoD/onshore sensor ASICs on 130-65nm U.S. nodes that are SRAM-limited
us_manufacturability: SkyWater Bloomington MN (S130) or Fab 25 Austin TX (130-65nm), 200mm. No oxide-semiconductor module exists at either (no announcement found 2026-11). Needs dedicated IGZO sputter or In2O3 ALD tools (~$4-10M) because of In/Ga/Zn contamination policy. Prototyping at Purdue Birck (200mm oxide BEOL, 2026-09) or NY CREATES Albany.
who_is_already_doing_this: imec (2T0C program since IEDM 2020), Kioxia, IMECAS, Macronix (3D 2T0C), Georgia Tech/Shimeng Yu (IWO eDRAM), Notre Dame/Datta (IWO 2T), Purdue/Ye & Li (ALD In2O3 3-layer 200mm), SEL (DOSRAM / OS-LSI; dominant oxide-semiconductor patent estate). Competing embedded memories already at U.S. foundries: Weebit ReRAM (SkyWater S130), MRAM at GlobalFoundries.
fatal_flaw: No U.S. foundry offers an oxide-semiconductor module. Adding one means dedicated tools ($4-10M) plus ~$10-30M and 3+ years of qualification [ESTIMATE]. PBTI is improving (imec IEDM 2025 abstract: 5-yr lifetime at 95C, 1.2 V overdrive, via snippet), but no 10-yr lifetime is shown, and IWO retention falls to ~300 ms at 85C, so refresh is mandatory. ASIC teams can already pick qualified Weebit ReRAM on S130, or a pure-CMOS Si gain cell (C-32) that needs no new module. SEL's estate is an FTO risk. Royalties on 130nm volumes are small.
possible: yes - cells demonstrated on 300mm, oxide BEOL demonstrated on a U.S. 200mm line (Purdue)
profitable: marginal - royalties on low-volume 130nm ASICs are small; the real money needs a 28nm-or-better foundry partner
doable_by_founder: no - process-module development and reliability qualification are far beyond <$50k and a day job

name: Standalone IGZO 2T0C DRAM die on a depreciated U.S. 200mm line (commodity DRAM substitute)
kill_reason: The card's own model puts standalone 4-tier IGZO 2T0C on 130nm at ~$336/GB. Against the canonical decks that is 21x the 4Q26 DDR5 contract price ($15.99), 52x the glut price ($6.40) and ~205x incumbent cost ($1.64). The card's '12x' used $27 spot. Its named buyer (industrial/legacy DDR4) pays for $/GB, and the card's wins_axis is 'none'. It would also take T3 capital to try. Even the hypothetical 300mm 28nm 4-tier version ($11.8/GB) is 1.8x the glut price and 7x incumbent cost, on a line no U.S. foundry offers.
wins_axis: none for commodity buyers (loses on $/GB, bandwidth, latency); refresh power only
buyer: (would be) industrial and legacy DDR4 buyers in the shortage, who will not pay ~12x DDR5 prices
us_manufacturability: SkyWater Fab 25 Austin (200mm, 130-65nm) technically could add IGZO tiers; 130nm litho is the binding constraint
who_is_already_doing_this: Nobody commercially at mature nodes; imec, IMECAS, Kioxia, SK hynix, and Samsung pursue oxide DRAM at leading-edge pitches
fatal_flaw: 130nm lithography gives ~120x lower bit density than 1b DRAM (0.0035 vs 0.436 Gb/mm2 with 4 tiers); stacking recovers only linear factors.
possible: yes - physics works (2T0C cells and 4-tier stacks are demonstrated)
profitable: no - $/GB ~21x the DDR5 contract price today, ~52x the glut price, ~205x incumbent cost

name: OCTRAM-class 4F2 IGZO-on-capacitor low-refresh DRAM as a U.S. second source
kill_reason: OCTRAM is a 4F2 IGZO transistor built on a high-aspect-ratio DRAM capacitor, so it needs a DRAM capacitor process. In the U.S. only Micron (Boise, Manassas, Clay) has one, and all of it is captive (01_LANDSCAPE 6.1 rows 1-3). The card itself sets capital at T4 and 84+ months, and Kioxia/Nanya do not offer the IP for license. Even at demo pitch the card's $8.4/GB is 5.1x incumbent cost ($1.64) and 1.3x the glut price.

buyer: mobile/IoT and AI-server low-power DRAM buyers (via DRAM makers), not a startup's customers
us_manufacturability: Requires a DRAM capacitor process => only Micron (Boise ID, Manassas VA) in the U.S.; Nanya (Taiwan) is Kioxia's partner. Violates rule 3 for us.
who_is_already_doing_this: Kioxia + Nanya (OCTRAM); Samsung (4F2 VCT with reportedly IGZO channel, 2028 target); SK hynix (4F2 vertical-gate DRAM at VLSI 2026)

possible: yes - for DRAM makers
profitable: no - not for a startup

name: License NEO Semiconductor 3D X-DRAM and build it in the U.S.
rule1_status: SUPPORTED-WEAK (company-reported single-cell PoC; no peer-reviewed array data)
kill_reason: Producing 3D X-DRAM needs a 3D-NAND-class fab ($10B-class, T4). No volume 3D NAND fab operates in the U.S., and NEO licenses to memory makers, so a startup cannot take the licensee seat. The evidence is also weak on R1. It is a single-cell, company-reported PoC (NYCU/TSRI test chips) with no peer-reviewed array data, and measured retention (>1 s at 85C) is ~450x below NEO's own earlier TCAD claim (>450 s).

who_is_already_doing_this: NEO Semiconductor (licensor), Samsung, SK hynix, Micron, Kioxia, imec, IMECAS
fatal_flaw: Single-cell, company-reported PoC with no peer-reviewed array data; production needs a $10B-class fab. NEO pitches to memory companies, so the licensee seat is not available to a startup.

Scorer verdicts — founder: A third-source FeRAM chip company in an incumbent-owned niche whose 'onshore' pitch fails because Infineon's die is already made in Dallas; it cannot be funded from a day job. | vc: Optane-style capital burn for a third-source slot in a hundreds-of-$M niche where Infineon already ships U.S.-fabbed QML-V F-RAM and HZO still trails PZT on endurance and hot retention. | veteran: HZO is the right ferroelectric and the physics is sound, but the 'onshore second source' story collapses because Infineon's F-RAM is already fabbed in Dallas, and a 54-month T2 module build makes this a funded-t

Sandia MESA for rad-hard pilot (CRADA/SPP, Ltd access). Note that the incumbent's Excelon die is already made in Dallas TX (TI DMOS6).
who_is_already_doing_this: Infineon (PZT F-RAM incl. QML-V rad-hard; Excelon die at TI Dallas DMOS6 300mm/130nm), RAMXEED (ex-Fujitsu; PZT 10-yr at 125C; active HZO R&D aimed at Gb-class FeRAM), TI (embedded FRAM), CEA-Leti (16-kb HZO FeRAM at 130nm; eFeRAM on 22nm FD-SOI, IEDM 2024), FMC (Germany), Sony/Fraunhofer/NaMLab, Sandia (MESA HZO). U.S.-made rad-tolerant alternatives: Everspin toggle MRAM (Chandler AZ) in Frontgrade modules; Honeywell/BAE trusted MRAM/SRAM.

Research arrays reach ~1e11 cycles and ~10-yr retention at 85C, versus 1e13-1e14 cycles and 10 yr at 125C (RAMXEED) or >100 yr at 85C (Infineon). The 'onshore second source' story is weak because Infineon's F-RAM die is already U.S.-fabbed (TI Dallas DMOS6) and U.S.-made toggle MRAM serves space. RAMXEED and CEA-Leti are pursuing HZO density themselves. The niche is ~hundreds of $M/yr [ESTIMATE] and incumbent-dominated.

name: FeFET embedded NVM licensing on GlobalFoundries 22FDX for U.S. MCU/edge SoCs

kill_reason: The card's only axis is supply security, and an unqualified U.S. startup improves it for none of the named buyers. Demand is soft too. Samsung's IGZO channel is only 'reported' (TrendForce 2026-04), and an Oct-2026 report says there is no fixed mass-production timetable. Micron, the only U.S. DRAM maker, is reported to be skipping 4F2 (snippets), so there is no onshore volume customer. Vertical-channel and stacked 3D IGZO also need conformal ALD, which makes 'DRAM-grade sputter targets' largely the wrong product [ESTIMATE: device-physics judgment].

name: DDR3-EOL Socket Swap to ST-DDR4 MRAM

kill_reason: The named buyer, an industrial, medical or rail OEM facing a DDR3 EOL, pays for continuity at the lowest respin cost, and MRAM loses on every axis of that purchase. On price, 1Gb ST-DDR4 sells at ~$821/GB street ($102.60 @500), ~32x DDR3 4Gb spot (~$25.5/GB). Modeled silicon is ~$95/GB, ~23x the $4.12/GB foundry DDR3 cost (01_LANDSCAPE 4.1). On density, one die is 1Gb. On compatibility, ST-DDR4 is not pin- or protocol-compatible with DDR3 (the card says so itself), so the 'swap' is a full respin, and a respin to DDR4/LPDDR4 is cheaper. That respin target is now U.S.-made: Micron Manassas 1-alpha DDR4, shipping since 2026-05-22, is aimed at exactly the long-lifecycle buyer and takes away the card's 'U.S. vendor roadmap' axis. Non-volatility is not needed for working DRAM; where it is needed (battery-backed SRAM), C-12 F-RAM or xSPI MRAM is the right part. The card itself says profitable: no.

Planar TCCT computes to ~$18/GB: above the $15.99 contract today, 2.8x the $6.40 glut and ~11x the $1.64 incumbent cost, and its 1-2 ns read is erased behind a DDR interface. The cache-macro variant has no real buyer at the U.S. nodes named. GF's U.S. SOI flows are RF-SOI and SkyWater 90nm FD-SOI is a rad-hard flow, neither of which hosts cache-hungry SoCs, and neither offers the 2-4-mask thyristor module. GF/AMD's own patent (US7630235) records TCCT-DRAM write-0 charge-loss disturb. A buyer who wants denser-than-SRAM cache at a U.S. node gets it with zero masks from gain cells (C-32), which RAAAM is now qualifying with GF.
wins_axis: Read latency (SRAM-class) and density vs SRAM. It does not win on $/GB vs DRAM except in the never-demonstrated VLT claim.
buyer: None identified: U.S. SOI flows (GF RF-SOI, SkyWater 90nm FD-SOI) serve RF and rad-hard parts, not cache-limited SoCs
us_manufacturability: A GF U.S. SOI flow or SkyWater Bloomington MN 90nm FD-SOI [UNVERIFIED-training]. Neither offers a thyristor module.
who_is_already_doing_this: Nobody commercially. GF dropped T-RAM. Synopsys owns the Kilopass assets and has not marketed VLT [UNVERIFIED-training]. There is some academic TCAD work on 3D thyristor DRAM.
fatal_flaw: The ON state needs a holding current. At 1-100 pA/cell a 1 Gb array idles at ~1-110 mA, and the bistable window shrinks at 85-125C. Three serious attempts failed to productize: AMD 2006, GlobalFoundries 2009, Kilopass 2016 [UNVERIFIED-training].
possible: marginal — TCCT arrays demonstrated, temperature/standby problems unsolved
profitable: no

name: Si gain-cell eDRAM (GCRAM) IP for U.S. trailing-node SoCs
subbranch: Capacitor-less silicon DRAM: 2T/3T gain-cell eDRAM in logic
rule1_status: SUPPORTED (industry sources: RAAAM/GF GCRAM, via search snippets)
wins_axis: On-chip memory density (bits/mm2) and standby leakage per bit vs 6T SRAM at equal process cost.
buyer: Edge-AI and sensor SoC teams on U.S. trailing nodes; DoD trusted-foundry ASIC programs; FPGA vendors needing denser block RAM.
us_manufacturability: SkyWater (an IonQ subsidiary since 2026-07-31; says it continues serving all foundry customers): Bloomington MN S130 / 90nm FD-SOI and Fab 25 Austin (65-130nm). GF Fab 8 Malta NY (12LP+). Test chips via ChipFoundry (buyer of Efabless's assets) or the Cadence/SkyWater open MPW. GF's own gain-cell program (RAAAM) is on FDX, which is made in Dresden, not the U.S.
who_is_already_doing_this: RAAAM Memory Technologies (Israel/Switzerland): $17.5M Series A led by NXP (2025); GF strategic collaboration with a GCRAM test vehicle taped out on FDX and lead-customer design access in early 2027; moving toward TSMC 2nm qualification; GCRAM reported from 180nm to 5nm (via search snippets). Academic groups at Bar-Ilan/EPFL (RAAAM's lineage) and Georgia Tech (oxide 3T). Incumbent SRAM compilers from Synopsys/Arm. C-01 covers oxide gain cells and C-43 covers cryo gain cells.
fatal_flaw: RAAAM already holds the commercial Si gain-cell position, with NXP money, GF and TSMC programs and silicon down to 180nm, and can address SkyWater S130 whenever it chooses. A new entrant starts with no silicon and must clear FTO against RAAAM/Bar-Ilan/EPFL patents. Trailing-node royalty pools are small (MoSys precedent), and 85-125C retention of ~10-100 us forces refresh that erodes the power claim.
possible: yes — silicon-proven in academia and at one startup
profitable: no to marginal: high-margin IP, but a small trailing-node royalty pool contested by a funded incumbent with foundry partnerships
doable_by_founder: no: needs a full-time memory-circuit cofounder, ~$2-5M and an FTO opinion before the founder's compiler/web tooling matters

buyer: University VLSI labs, DoD SBIR/STTR ASIC teams needing U.S.-only fabrication, hardware startups on ChipFoundry/SkyWater shuttles.
us_manufacturability: Customer silicon is made at SkyWater Bloomington MN (S130; SkyWater has been an IonQ subsidiary since 2026-07-31 and says it keeps serving foundry customers) via ChipFoundry MPW or the Cadence/SkyWater open MPW (2026: Jan submission, July die). doable_by_founder: yes — T0, software-led, starts alongside the day job

name: Depreciated-fab revival of IBM-heritage deep-trench eDRAM
subbranch: 1T1C eDRAM at foundries; depreciated trailing-edge capacity
kill_reason: Even at depreciated cash-cost wafers the card computes ~$20/GB standalone (~$50/GB at a normal wafer price). That compares with the $15.99 contract, the $6.40 glut and the $1.64 incumbent cost, because density is 0.026 vs 0.436 Gb/mm2 (17x). Its one axis, a ~2 ns macro cycle, disappears behind a DDR interface for the standalone die (the C-35 logic). The LLC-chiplet buyer is self-labeled 'hypothetical', and SRAM chiplets and 3D-stacked SRAM already serve it. There is also no host: IBM moved POWER10/z16 to Samsung 7nm without eDRAM, East Fishkill is an onsemi fab, and GF no longer offers 14HP [UNVERIFIED-training], so a restart is a T3 process rebuild with the tool set and know-how dispersed.
wins_axis: None for a real buyer. Latency is lost behind DDR I/O, and the LLC-chiplet buyer is hypothetical and served by SRAM/3D-SRAM.
buyer: HPC/ASIC teams wanting a fast on-package cache tier (hypothetical).
us_manufacturability: No U.S. line runs deep-trench eDRAM (East Fishkill is onsemi's; GF 14HP not offered [UNVERIFIED-training]). Would require a T3 module rebuild.
who_is_already_doing_this: Nobody. IBM exited eDRAM with POWER10/z16. Intel ended Crystalwell-class eDRAM. GF no longer offers 14HP [UNVERIFIED-training].
fatal_flaw: Depreciation cannot close a 17x density gap: wafer cost is a minor term once density is 0.026 vs 0.436 Gb/mm2. The tool set and know-how are likely gone [UNVERIFIED-training].
possible: marginal — it shipped before, but the process is retired
profitable: no — density gap dominates even at cash-cost wafers

name: Trailing-node bulk SRAM as a DRAM substitute (SRAM-DIMM/CXL)
kill_reason: The card itself names no winning axis and no buyer. SRAM silicon is ~$55-72/GB at 7-28nm (01_LANDSCAPE s4.4), or ~$80-120/GB with test per A3. That is 3.5-7.5x the $15.99/GB contract, 9-19x the $6.40 glut and 35-70x the $1.64 incumbent cost. Refresh-free operation and latency are lost behind a DDR4/CXL controller (~50-100 ns). A 1 Gb SRAM die needs ~181 mm2 at 28nm, and the only U.S. option (GF Malta 12/14nm) does not change the cost floor.
wins_axis: None at a DRAM interface: the latency advantage is lost behind the DDR/CXL controller (~50-100 ns), and it loses on $/GB by 3-40x.
buyer: None identified. A DRAM buyer will not pay 4x spot for refresh-free capacity.
us_manufacturability: GF Fab 8 Malta NY (12/14nm) is the closest U.S. option. 28nm SRAM die is otherwise Taiwan-made.
who_is_already_doing_this: Nobody sells SRAM as bulk DRAM capacity. SRAM capacity is sold only as on-die memory (Groq, Cerebras, see C-38/C-39) or small standalone parts (C-36).
fatal_flaw: SRAM has a ~$80-120/GB silicon+test cost floor at every node from 28nm to N2. SRAM cell scaling has stalled, so trailing nodes are not cheaper per SRAM bit: 40nm is ~$144/GB and 65nm ~$268/GB.
possible: yes — trivially manufacturable
profitable: no — 4x above today's spot, ~10x above glut

In RAG, retrieval energy is a small share next to LLM inference on GPUs.

name: Memory-only wafer-scale SRAM ('Cerebras for RAM')
subbranch: Wafer-scale SRAM as a RAM product
kill_reason: The card itself names no winning axis and no buyer. A 28nm memory-only wafer holds ~27 GB at ~$111/GB in silicon and ~$1,000/GB packaged. That is ~63x the $15.99/GB 4Q26 DDR5 contract price and ~156x the $6.40/GB glut. On-wafer bandwidth must leave through an ~860 mm perimeter of SerDes/CXL, so the host sees CXL-class latency and bandwidth: no latency, bandwidth or density gain. It even holds less SRAM than Cerebras WSE-3 (44 GB, with compute on the same wafer). Wafer-scale yield via redundancy is real (Cerebras), but that is not the issue.
wins_axis: None for a host: on-wafer bandwidth cannot leave the wafer through an ~860 mm perimeter.
buyer: None identified. Latency-critical buyers buy Cerebras/Groq compute instead.
us_manufacturability: No U.S. 28nm host. GF Malta offers 12/14nm FinFET (higher wafer cost). U.S. wafer-scale packaging is unproven [UNVERIFIED].
who_is_already_doing_this: Cerebras (compute + SRAM on one wafer, TSMC). Nobody sells memory-only wafers.
fatal_flaw: Cerebras's economics come from co-locating compute with SRAM. A memory-only wafer exports its bandwidth through edge I/O, so it is DRAM at 40-100x the price with no latency advantage visible to the host.
possible: yes — engineering-feasible
profitable: no

kill_reason: For the card's own buyer (space primes buying rad-hard NVM), a 1T1R NRAM in SkyWater S130 wins no axis. The cell's claimed high-temperature and radiation tolerance is hidden behind the bulk-CMOS access transistor and periphery (~125-150 C, not rad-hard-by-process). On density, speed and endurance it at best ties qualified Toggle MRAM, rad-hard F-RAM and Weebit 1T1R ReRAM, which is already qualified in the same S130 process (C-22), while being ~48 months and a T2 qualification program behind. The licensor looks dormant. Two searches found no Nantero product, license or funding news after the 2016 Fujitsu/Mie Fujitsu deal, whose end-2018 product never appeared. The 'DDR-class' pitch is ~$31/GB even at a hypothetical 28nm (no U.S. host), vs $6.40/GB glut DDR5.

buyer: Space primes and rad-hard component distributors (Frontgrade-type channel); downhole/high-temperature industrial.
us_manufacturability: SkyWater Bloomington MN (S130 BEOL) or Fab 25 Austin. The licensor is in Massachusetts (East Coast).
who_is_already_doing_this: Nantero (no public license, product or funding news found for 2024-2026; STILL-UNVERIFIED whether operating). Fujitsu/Mie Fujitsu licensees (2016; no product). Same-fab competitor: Weebit ReRAM qualified in SkyWater S130 (C-22). Rad-hard incumbents: Everspin Toggle MRAM via Frontgrade, Infineon rad-hard F-RAM, Honeywell/BAE.
fatal_flaw: 20+ years and >$100M [UNVERIFIED-training] without a known volume product; the Fujitsu-licensed product apparently never shipped. In rad-hard it must displace qualified Toggle MRAM and F-RAM incumbents.
possible: marginal — demonstrated by licensees, never productized
profitable: no — no evidence of a cost or performance win that incumbents can't match

name: 2D-material (MoS2/WSe2) gain-cell DRAM or 2D flash
rule1_status: SUPPORTED at device/small-array scale; UNSUPPORTED at product scale
kill_reason: The card names no buyer ('None until TRL 6+') and no production partner. Penn State 2DCC and NY CREATES are research venues, and neither gap can be closed within the >96-month horizon. The card also misreads its evidence. Fudan's 400 ps PoX (Nature 641:90-97, 2025) is a graphene-channel flash, not MoS2/WSe2. Its Oct-2025 2D-flash+CMOS chip is a small demonstrator (94.3% cell yield) with MB scale targeted in 3-5 years, at a Chinese university. Mechanism evidence exists at device and small-array scale (TRL 3-4), so R1 is not the reason. The reason is no buyer, no U.S. fab and no shown axis over IGZO 2T0C (R4 also applies).
wins_axis: Retention per area (speculative) — not demonstrated at array scale.
buyer: None until TRL 6+.
us_manufacturability: No U.S. production line; research only (Penn State 2DCC, NY CREATES Albany).
who_is_already_doing_this: Academic groups (Fudan, Penn State, MIT, Stanford); TSMC/imec/Intel 2D-channel logic research [UNVERIFIED-training].
fatal_flaw: No defect-controlled, wafer-scale 2D growth at BEOL-compatible temperature, and no array-scale demonstration. Contact resistance and variability are unsolved. IGZO (C-01..04) already delivers the low-leakage benefit on 300mm today.
possible: no (not within the venture horizon) — lab devices only; UNSUPPORTED at array scale
profitable: no

kill_reason: ~$4x10^7/GB by label cost (A3 model) is ~6.8 orders of magnitude above $6.40/GB glut DDR5. It also has ms latency, 10^3-10^5 endurance and high-voltage programming. The pioneer (Thin Film Electronics) left printed memory for NFC and then microbatteries as Ensurge [UNVERIFIED-training; not re-checked, quota spent on survival-relevant cards]. The mechanism is real for bit-level labels, so the rule is R4, not R1.

fatal_flaw: Density, latency and endurance are each 6-10 orders of magnitude from RAM. The company that pioneered it abandoned memory twice and later failed [UNVERIFIED-training].
possible: no as RAM (UNSUPPORTED for any RAM role; 20-bit labels did ship, no URL retrievable this session)
profitable: no

name: Cryo-CMOS gain-cell eDRAM IP for quantum-computer control
kill_reason: Same idea as C-32: a zero-extra-mask Si 2T/3T gain-cell eDRAM compiler/IP on SkyWater S90 FD-SOI and GF 12LP+, licensed for NRE plus royalty. The only difference is a 4 K characterization deck and a quantum-controller buyer list. That is a C-32 product line costing ~$50-150k of dilution-fridge time [ESTIMATE], not a separate venture, and its market is a few dozen quantum teams, most designing in-house. Physics is better than the card says (TRL 4): a 16 Kb 4T gain cell keeps >16.6 s at 4.2 K (ISCAS 2023 / US 12412613), a 4 Kb 40nm cell keeps 66.5 s (arXiv 2311.11572), and a 28nm 3T1C runs at 4 K (ISOCC 2024). If C-32 is killed elsewhere, re-score C-43 as KEEP_WITH_CORRECTIONS with the corrections below; it does not fail on physics.
wins_axis: Static power at the 4 K stage and memory density for cryo control electronics.
buyer: Quantum computing hardware teams (IBM Quantum NY, Google Quantum AI), DARPA/IARPA quantum programs.
us_manufacturability: GF Fab 8 Malta NY (12LP+) or SkyWater Bloomington MN (90nm FD-SOI). Cryo test needs a dilution refrigerator, rented from a university or national lab.
who_is_already_doing_this: In-house cryo-CMOS teams (Intel Horse Ridge, IBM, Google, imec); academic cryo gain-cell groups (ShanghaiTech and other Chinese groups; Bar-Ilan/BGU, the academic lineage of RAAAM [UNVERIFIED-training]); SEEQC (SFQ). RAAAM, the C-32 competitor, is the natural owner of this extension.
fatal_flaw: The market is a few dozen teams, most of which design memory in-house. Quantum roadmaps may keep control at room temperature for years. It needs a cryo test lab and a circuit designer.
possible: yes — physics favorable
profitable: no as a standalone company — the market is a few dozen teams

possible: yes: production at Moonshot; all parts off-the-shelf

Against every alternative its buyer can actually get, free or purchasable, the FPGA card wins no axis. That is the same test that killed C-77.

Scorer verdicts — founder: Merchant silicon (Structera X) and ZeroPoint's ASIC licensee already do this more cheaply, and the glut wipes out the savings; dead for this founder. | vc: An FPGA integrator of non-exclusive compression IP fighting Marvell's ASIC that already does the job, and the savings stop covering the card in a glut: dead on arrival. | veteran: An FPGA integrator of non-exclusive IP that Marvell already put in merchant silicon; the DRAM saving that pays for the card is gone at the $8.15 glut.

name: Rack-Scale CXL Pooling Appliance
kill_reason: The card's only axis is fleet $/GB from recovering stranded memory, and its own literature says a switch-based design loses money on that axis. Pond (ASPLOS '23) gets ~7% gross DRAM saving at 16 sockets (7-9% on the poster), from emulation on Azure traces, and uses an external memory controller specifically to avoid switch latency. Octopus (Azure plus universities, arXiv 2501.09020) finds CXL switches produce a net server-cost increase and only 3-5.4% net saving for the best switchless topology. Google's HotNets '23 'A Case Against CXL Memory Pooling' argues cabling and switching cost more than multiplexing saves (all via search snippet). For a 16-socket, 12 TB pod, 7-9% is ~$17-22k at the 4Q26 deck and ~$7-9k in the glut, before switch, controllers, cables and a 1-5% slowdown [ESTIMATE]. Mainline Linux (opened, 2026-10-31) still scores Dynamic Capacity, multi-host sharing and fabrics [0], so the dynamic reallocation the saving depends on is unsupported. C-76 was already killed as a duplicate of this card, so this verdict covers the pooling idea in both forms.
wins_axis: Stranded-memory reduction (fleet $/GB)
buyer: Hyperscale and large VM cloud operators
us_manufacturability: Switch/controller silicon from TSMC; chassis assembly could be U.S.
who_is_already_doing_this: Liqid (composable memory), GigaIO, XConn, Panmnesia (CXL 3.x switch), Unifabrix (status unknown), H3 Platform, Astera Labs, Enfabrica (NVIDIA acqui-hire Sep 2025) [all UNVERIFIED-T]
fatal_flaw: The OS is not ready: mainline Linux (2026-10-31) still lists Dynamic Capacity, multi-host sharing and fabrics as [0] known gaps. The only buyers big enough to benefit build their own, and Pond's own result was single-digit-percent savings.
possible: marginal: switches exist (XConn, Panmnesia), but dynamic multi-host capacity has no mainline OS support (DCD/sharing [0]) and switch-based pooling is net-cost-negative in Azure's own Octopus analysis
profitable: no

kill_reason: Scored 53.0/100 default (rank 32/40), 50.8 moonshot. rule1_status: UNSUPPORTED (value claim): no evidence any HPC/defense buyer pays a premium for U.S.-fabbed DRAM. 01_LANDSCAPE 7.3 finds none

It describes itself as a fabless maker of pin-for-pin drop-in DRAM/SRAM with long-term support, and its DDR4 8Gb AS4C1G8D4 is in distribution (via search snippets). Intelligent Memory, Etron and Zentel do the same. A newcomer sells the same lifecycle axis with no track record, ~$15M of NRE and first revenue at 36-48 months, past the 36-month ceiling, so the named industrial/avionics buyer gets worse price, availability and longevity credibility. The supply premise is also weakening: PSMC, the named DRAM foundry, is selling its Tongluo fab to Micron ($1.8B LOI, Jan-2026), taking a Micron 1Y license and phasing out low-margin legacy products (via search snippet).
wins_axis: none vs incumbents: the same lifecycle/supply-security axis Alliance Memory and Intelligent Memory already sell, with no track record and worse wafer access
buyer: Industrial-PC, networking, medical-imaging and avionics OEMs with 10-20-year product lives
us_manufacturability: Essentially none: wafers in Taiwan (PSMC Hsinchu/Tongluo [UNVERIFIED-training]), packaging and test in Asia. TAA-compliant through Taiwan wafer origin; cannot claim 'Made in USA'.
who_is_already_doing_this: Alliance Memory (U.S.-based fabless legacy DRAM brand; 'long-term support'; DDR4 8Gb AS4C1G8D4 in distribution; stock in U.S./Shanghai/Taiwan), Intelligent Memory, Etron, Zentel, ISSI. PSMC's DRAM foundry capacity is shifting toward Micron (Tongluo sale, 1Y license).
fatal_flaw: This is Alliance Memory's business model with no history, ~$15M NRE and 36-48 months to revenue. Its named foundry (PSMC) is pivoting its DRAM capacity to Micron and phasing out low-margin legacy work, so a newcomer gets wafers only after prices collapse.
possible: yes technically; newcomer wafer supply doubtful as PSMC's DRAM capacity moves to Micron
profitable: marginal - margins depend on wafer allocation the newcomer will not get in a shortage
doable_by_founder: no - T2 hardware program with Taiwan-centric operations

name: 'Assembled in USA' commodity DDR4/DDR5 module brand (tempting, dead)
kill_reason: The card itself gives wins_axis as 'None that is paid for'. Per 01_LANDSCAPE: U.S. assembly adds $8.63 per 64GB RDIMM, 0.7% of a $1,300 contract module (4.2). TAA treats Korean and Taiwanese DRAM as compliant, Section 232 charges memory 0%, and the FTC allows only 'Assembled in USA' on foreign die (7.3). Without die allocation the brand buys components at street prices and competes with Kingston, PNY and the Taiwanese module houses at a 5-15% margin. Landscape 10.2 lists this path as closed, and C-70, the all-domestic variant, was already killed.
wins_axis: None that is paid for: 'assembled in USA' is not an axis buyers reward
buyer: Consumer upgraders and small federal buys (BAA)
us_manufacturability: Easy: Kingston (Fountain Valley CA) and Virtium (Rancho Santa Margarita CA) assemble in the U.S., and any U.S. EMS can SMT a DIMM [UNVERIFIED-training].
who_is_already_doing_this: Kingston (dominant independent), Virtium, SMART Modular (Penguin), PNY (NJ), OWC, plus Taiwanese houses (ADATA, TeamGroup, G.Skill).
fatal_flaw: Assembly is ~0.6-1.0% of a 2026 64GB RDIMM's cost (Appendix A), TAA treats Taiwan/Korea as compliant and the FTC bars an unqualified Made-in-USA claim on foreign die, while the 93-98% that matters - die - is allocated away from small module makers; Netlist's PMIC/rank patents also read on new DDR5 RDIMM brands.
possible: yes - trivial to assemble
profitable: no - no die allocation, no paid premium, patent exposure

name: DRAM Continuity Vault: consignment last-time-buy storage plus LTB-sizing software
wins_axis: Lifecycle length / supply security
buyer: Mid-size OEMs with 10-30-year field lives (industrial PCs, rail signaling, grid-protection relays, medical imaging, avionics retrofit) too small for Rochester's re-creation programs
us_manufacturability: A 2,000-4,000 sq ft ESD- and climate-controlled vault on the East Coast; no fab dependency; U.S.-made DDR4 from Micron Manassas can be the stored part where OEMs want domestic origin.
who_is_already_doing_this: Rochester Electronics (die/wafer banking, Newburyport MA), Micross (die banking; long-term storage guidance), Semitron (DE, nitrogen long-term packaging of customer-supplied stock), Astute Group (nitrogen/humidity-controlled storage), Super Dry/Totech (OEM in-house dry-storage systems), distributor bonded inventory (Arrow, Avnet), HTV (DE); lifecycle data from SiliconExpert and Z2Data
fatal_flaw: Trust, scale and cheap substitutes. OEMs hand $0.5-2M of critical inventory only to an insured vault with a record. Incumbents (Rochester, Micross, distributor bonded stock, Semitron/Astute) already store parts. An OEM can buy an N2 dry cabinet for ~$5k and store in-house, which caps the 4%/yr fee. Breakeven needs ~8-10 OEMs.
possible: yes - component long-term storage and die banking exist
profitable: marginal-to-no until ~10+ OEMs; ~27% GM at 10
doable_by_founder: marginal - software-first start is feasible; the vault needs a partner or hire

name: ProvenRAM: graded, serialized recovered server RDIMMs
wins_axis: $/GB (used at roughly 25-60% of new) plus documented test provenance
buyer: Third-party maintenance firms keeping DDR4 fleets alive, small cloud/HPC/CPU-offload inference operators, university labs; not DoD (DFARS 252.246-7008 / FAR 52.211-5 bar used parts without contracting-officer approval [UNVERIFIED-training])
us_manufacturability: U.S. test-and-grade bench in East Coast flex space; the U.S. value-add is testing and documentation, not manufacturing.
who_is_already_doing_this: ServerMonkey, Memory4Less, TechMikeNY (NYC), BuySellRAM, Curvature/Park Place, ITADs selling direct, Mobius Materials (authenticated marketplace, Richmond VA) and thousands of eBay sellers.
fatal_flaw: No moat and a closing window. The resale spread is a bet on DDR4 prices that peak in 2026-27, so the line must be cash-positive by end-2027 (01_LANDSCAPE F2). ITADs sell direct, and hyperscalers reuse DDR4 behind CXL. The serialized ledger is copyable because SPD already holds an assembly serial that decode-dimms prints. DoD is closed (DFARS 252.246-7008).
possible: yes - an existing U.S. trade
profitable: yes in 2026-27 / no in a glut - ~20% contribution now, ~1-6% in the A-05 glut

name: Die harvesting and module rebuild from e-waste, Shenzhen-style (tempting, dead)
kill_reason: The card's own model says rebuilding destroys value. An intact, tested 32GB RDIMM is worth ~$192, against ~$72 of harvested x4 chips before a new PCB, RCD, assembly and 5-10% reball fallout. At the A-05 glut a harvested chip ($2.5) is worth less than its rework cost ($3.6). For the named price-sensitive buyer, an intact used module (C-62) beats a rebuilt one on price, reliability and legality. Reballed parts read as suspect counterfeits under AS6171, and x4 server die fit only RDIMMs (01_LANDSCAPE 6.3, 10.2). The only viable fragment, disclosed BGA repair, is already folded into C-62.
wins_axis: $/GB (nominal)
buyer: Price-sensitive consumer and legacy-platform buyers
us_manufacturability: Possible with a BGA rework station and X-ray in any U.S. shop; uncompetitive on labor versus Shenzhen.
who_is_already_doing_this: Shenzhen/Huaqiangbei refurbishers; in the U.S. only disclosed board-level repair shops.
fatal_flaw: Geometry and law: server RDIMMs carry x4 dies that only fit other RDIMMs, an intact tested 32GB module is worth ~2.7x its harvested chips ($192 vs ~$72), reballed parts read as counterfeits under AS6171, and selling them as new is a crime under 18 U.S.C. 2320. The only surviving fragment - disclosed BGA repair of failed RDIMMs with tested donor chips - is folded into C-62.
possible: yes - done at scale in China
profitable: no - in the U.S. at U.S. labor rates and legal standards
doable_by_founder: no - legal exposure outweighs any margin

name: CleanBOM-5949: memory-provenance verification for federal IT sellers
subbranch: Government preference as moat (NDAA Sec. 5949 compliance)
rule1_status: PARTIAL - statute and FAR Case 2023-008 confirmed; demand for independent verification is NOT supported by the proposed rule (certification after reasonable inquiry, no third-party audit, no affirmative proof, safe harbor for reliance on supplier certifications)
wins_axis: Supply security / provenance assurance
buyer: Primary: server/PC/appliance OEMs and ODMs, DIMM/SSD module makers and federal systems integrators that must certify upstream and need die-level knowledge. Secondary: GSA MAS/SEWP resellers, who under the 5949(h) safe harbor will mostly rely on OEM certifications and pay little.
us_manufacturability: Software and services; physical die-ID sampling at U.S. independent counterfeit-test labs; no fab dependency (rubric: software/services).
who_is_already_doing_this: No memory-specific Sec. 5949 product found in a 2026-11-01 search [UNVERIFIED]. Adjacent: government-contracts law firms advising on 5949 (Crowell, Wiley, Covington, Mayer Brown, DLA Piper, Reed Smith), supply-chain-illumination vendors (Exiger, Interos, Govini), component-risk data (SiliconExpert, Z2Data), teardown die-ID (TechInsights), counterfeit-test labs (SMT Corp, Micross), OEM self-certification (Dell, HP, Lenovo).
fatal_flaw: Now largely confirmed. The proposed FAR rule (2026-02-17) is certification-based, requires no third-party audit or proof artifacts, and gives a safe harbor for relying on supplier certifications, as Section 889 did. Most sellers can self-attest at near-zero cost. Paid demand shrinks to OEM/module makers and risk-averse integrators. Large compliance-data vendors can add a CXMT flag, and the SPD scanner is commodity code. The final rule could tighten or loosen this.
possible: yes - SPD reads and die-ID teardowns are routine; the integration is new
profitable: marginal-to-no - ~70% GM on software, but the certification-based rule and safe harbor cut the paying population well below the card's 37 customers
doable_by_founder: yes - T0 software-plus-partner-lab start, part-time feasible

name: U.S. hi-rel DDR4/LPDDR4 multi-chip memory design house
subbranch: Packaging-only: hi-rel MCM from purchased KGD
wins_axis: Lifecycle length, environmental ruggedness, traceability
buyer: Defense primes' mission computers, NewSpace avionics, rugged industrial system-on-modules
us_manufacturability: U.S. assembly and screening at hi-rel OSATs (Micross, QP Technologies, Integra) of imported die. Winbond/ESMT KGD is open. Micron die reaches established hi-rel houses (Teledyne e2v uses it), but startup access through Micross/SpecTek is UNVERIFIED (Micross line card does not name Micron, 01_LANDSCAPE row 23).
who_is_already_doing_this: Teledyne e2v DDR4T04G72 (4GB/8GB x72 ECC rad-tolerant DDR4 MCM on Micron die, 15x20 mm, -55 to 125 C, NASA Level 1/ECSS Class 1, since 2020), Micross, Mercury Systems, Data Device Corp, Frontgrade, 3D Plus (HEICO), Intelligent Memory
fatal_flaw: The flagship SKU already ships. Teledyne e2v has sold an x72 ECC 4/8GB DDR4 MCM with NASA Level 1 heritage since 2020, and Micross, DDC, Mercury, Frontgrade and 3D Plus hold flight and field heritage. Qualification plus design-in takes 30-42 months, and Micross is both a die/OSAT supplier and a competitor.
possible: yes - incumbents ship these
profitable: yes for incumbents with heritage; unproven for a no-heritage entrant
doable_by_founder: no - hardware team and qualification timeline

name: High-capacity stacked-die legacy modules (32GB DDR3 RDIMM, 32GB DDR3L SODIMM)
kill_reason: The card says it will build DDR3 capacities 'the majors never made or have stopped making'. That is false for both SKUs. Intelligent Memory's Oct-2024 DDR3 flyer and its product page list 32GB DDR3 RDIMM and LRDIMM modules built on its own 8Gb DDR3 parts, plus 16GB SO-DIMMs, which it has shipped since 2014. Samsung, SK hynix and Micron made the 8Gb dual-die DDR3 that 32GB RDIMMs use before those parts went EOL, so new and recovered supply of this exact module already exists (all via search snippets). The flagship 32GB DDR3L SO-DIMM cannot be built. JEDEC caps a SO-DIMM at 16 devices (PCWorld), and DDR3 devices top out at 8Gb [training: JESD79-3], so 16GB is the ceiling. What is left is a me-too module line. It would pay ~$788 per module for 4Gb KGD plus OSAT DDP, against an incumbent that owns the 8Gb component.
wins_axis: none vs. incumbent: the same density and lifecycle, at a worse cost position (bought 4Gb KGD + OSAT DDP vs. an incumbent-owned 8Gb part)
buyer: Telecom/network-equipment operators, industrial-PC fleets, legacy-server owners
us_manufacturability: Partial: DDP stacking in the U.S. only at low-volume hi-rel houses (Micross); otherwise Asia; module SMT at any U.S. EMS.
who_is_already_doing_this: Intelligent Memory ships 32GB DDR3 RDIMM/LRDIMM and 16GB DDR3(L) SO-DIMM/UDIMM on its own 8Gb DDR3 components (flyer 10.2024; first 16GB modules in 2014). Majors made 8Gb dual-die DDR3 (Samsung/SK hynix/Micron, now EOL), so recovered 32GB DDR3 RDIMMs circulate. Alliance, Virtium and ATP sell legacy modules.
fatal_flaw: A shrinking installed base, an incumbent (Intelligent Memory), and per-platform signal-integrity/BIOS validation that a small team cannot amortize.
possible: no for 32GB DDR3L SO-DIMM; yes for 32GB DDR3 RDIMM, but the incumbent already ships it
profitable: marginal - thin margins on a shrinking base
doable_by_founder: no - hardware engineering and die access

name: Rugged and new-form-factor memory modules built at a U.S. EMS (LPCAMM2/CAMM2, wide-temp coated SODIMM)
wins_axis: Environmental reliability, lifecycle, form factor
buyer: Rugged-computer makers (General Micro Systems, Crystal Group, Curtiss-Wright, Kontron-class) and defense primes
us_manufacturability: U.S. assembly of imported die (rubric 3). DDR5 and LPDDR5X die come from Asian fabs. Only DDR4/LPDDR4 SKUs can carry U.S.-fabbed Manassas die, and Micron's back-end is in Malaysia/India, so even those die are packaged offshore [REPORTED via snippet]. Conformal coat, screening and SMT are routine at U.S. Class-3 EMS.
who_is_already_doing_this: Virtium, SMART Modular (Penguin), Mercury Systems, ATP, Swissbit, Cervoz. Innodisk ships rugged screw-lock DDR5 and LPDDR5X CAMM2 (launched 2025-08). congatec ships rugged COM Express with screw-locked LPCAMM2 at -40 to +85 C (2026-04). Micron, Samsung and SK hynix make LPCAMM2/SOCAMM themselves.
fatal_flaw: Crowded by funded specialists (Virtium, SMART, ATP, Innodisk, which already ships rugged CAMM2) that compete for the same scarce component allocation. Design wins take 12-24 months. Memory makers ship CAMM-class modules themselves. U.S. content is limited to DDR4/LPDDR4 SKUs.
possible: yes - shipping category
profitable: marginal - 20-35% against strong incumbents

name: HBM-adjacent U.S. test and rework services near Amkor Peoria / SK hynix West Lafayette (dead for this founder)
rule1_status: UNSUPPORTED (value claim): no evidence that HBM makers outsource KGSD test, FA or rework
kill_reason: Every named customer is captive and closed to outside vendors. 01_LANDSCAPE.md 6.1 marks SK hynix West Lafayette (cleanroom Oct-2028, HBM4E from Q3-2029) and Micron's U.S. HBM packaging (2029+) as 'No' for outside customers (rows 19-20). Amkor Peoria integrates HBM into logic 2.5D packages but does not stack it, so it has no HBM-stack test or rework flow to serve (row 21) [UNVERIFIED]. The card admits both plants arrive with their own Advantest/Teradyne testers and Korean/Taiwanese suppliers. It gives no evidence that any HBM maker outsources KGSD test, and it puts first revenue at ~48 months, past the 36-month ceiling, on a T3 ticket. HBM 'rework' is also not a production flow: a failed TC-bonded stack or HBM-on-interposer assembly is scrapped [ESTIMATE: practitioner judgment]. 01_LANDSCAPE.md 10.2 already lists HBM packaging as closed.
wins_axis: Bandwidth supply (HBM) via local proximity
buyer: SK hynix Indiana and Micron Idaho (both captive, in-house test). Remove Amkor Peoria: logic 2.5D that integrates HBM and does not stack it.
us_manufacturability: Arizona/Indiana from 2028-29, but both plants are captive and arrive with their own Advantest/Teradyne HBM testers ($3-5M each [ESTIMATE]) and Korean/Taiwanese supplier ecosystems.
who_is_already_doing_this: SK hynix, Micron and Samsung in-house; Amkor, SPIL, ASE; Advantest, Teradyne, FormFactor; Hanmi, Hanwha and ASMPT for TC bonders [UNVERIFIED-training].
fatal_flaw: Captive, capital-heavy and late: no outside customer exists before 2028-29, the first customers bring incumbent suppliers, and the ticket is tens of millions.
possible: no for an outside vendor (captive flows); yes only in-house for SK hynix/Micron
profitable: marginal - only for incumbents

name: U.S. known-good-die wafer-probe and die-processing house for legacy DRAM
kill_reason: The gap this card would fill is already filled by the company it names as its buyer. Micross in Apopka, FL offers wafer probe, wafer mapping and inking, and die processing: ~850 wafers probed a year and over 37M die probed a year, in 29,000 sq ft of Class H/K cleanroom, AS9100 (Micross facility page and die/wafer flyer, via search snippets). That capacity exceeds both the card's own ~700-wafer/yr breakeven and the few hundred wafers a year of U.S. demand it estimates. The real choke point is die supply, not probe capacity (01_LANDSCAPE.md 6.3). Winbond, ESMT and Etron already ship JESD49B.01-tested KGD, and untested DRAM wafers are mostly not sold to outsiders (the card's own fatal flaw), so a second house would have no input and no winning axis.
wins_axis: none: U.S. location, AS9100 and probe capacity are already offered by Micross
buyer: Remove Micross: it is the incumbent provider, not a buyer. Mercury, DDC and SiP startups already buy tested KGD.
us_manufacturability: Yes in principle: any U.S. light-industrial cleanroom; probe cards and test programs cost $50-150k per die type [ESTIMATE].
who_is_already_doing_this: Micross Apopka FL (wafer probe ~850 wafers/yr, >37M die probed/yr, mapping/inking, AS9100) plus Rochester, ISE Labs (ASE), Integra and STS. The die vendors (Winbond, ESMT, Etron) ship tested KGD themselves.
fatal_flaw: Demand is a few hundred wafers a year, Winbond/ESMT/Etron already ship tested KGD, and untested DRAM wafers are mostly not sold to outsiders, so the house would sit idle.
possible: yes
profitable: no - below breakeven volume for the foreseeable market

name: All-domestic DRAM component: Micron Manassas wafer to U.S. package to U.S. module
subbranch: Module assembly and test in the U.S. (domestic-origin)
rule1_status: UNSUPPORTED (value claim): no buyer evidence for a domestic-origin premium. Landscape 7.3 finds none
kill_reason: The core value claim is that DoD and critical-infrastructure buyers will pay 1.5-3x for end-to-end U.S.-origin COTS DRAM. The card cites no evidence for it, and the canonical landscape contradicts it. TAA treats Korean and Taiwanese DRAM as compliant, COTS is exempt from the BAA component test, memory pays 0% under Section 232, and hi-rel buyers already pay 10-100x for MCMs built on foreign die (01_LANDSCAPE.md 0 item 7, 7.3). The card itself puts GM at ~0% without the premium. The supply side is unproven too. Manassas takes no outside customers (6.1 row 2). SpecTek lists wafers as a format but gives no availability or terms (via search snippet). Micron runs its back-end in Malaysia and India and could add U.S. packaging itself. The concept comes back only if two things happen: a written program requirement for U.S.-fabbed and U.S.-packaged DRAM, and a SpecTek 'yes' on Manassas wafers.
wins_axis: Supply security / domestic origin
buyer: DoD programs with domestic or trusted-sourcing clauses, critical-infrastructure agencies, a 'Made in USA' consumer niche
us_manufacturability: Fully U.S. only if Micron releases Manassas wafers. Today Micron's assembly/test hubs are Malaysia and India (TrendForce 2026-05-27, via snippet).
who_is_already_doing_this: Micron itself (U.S. fab, CHIPS-funded, could add domestic back-end at any time); Micross (U.S. hi-rel packaging of purchased die)
fatal_flaw: Gatekeeper risk: Micron decides whether Manassas silicon reaches outsiders in wafer form, and a paid premium for U.S.-packaged COTS DRAM is unproven because TAA/BAA treat Taiwan and Korea as compliant and memory carries no Section 232 tariff.
possible: unknown - gated by Micron/SpecTek releasing Manassas wafers (no public terms)
profitable: marginal - premium unproven

name: Trusted low-density SDRAM (64-512Mb) on SkyWater Fab 25 with 1T1C MIM cells
subbranch: Trailing-node DRAM on a U.S. pure-play foundry
kill_reason: For the named buyer (DoD DMSMS offices and avionics primes) the part loses on price: ~$30 unit cost and a $40-60 ASP against $2-5 COTS SDRAM that Winbond, ISSI and Alliance still make. It also loses on lifecycle, because SDRAM is still in production and Rochester re-creates EOL parts. The one axis it adds, a trusted U.S. fab, is not required for commodity memory: DoDI 5200.44 targets custom ICs, and COTS memory is bought commercially (01_LANDSCAPE.md 7.3). Where DoD does pay for trusted memory at SkyWater, it funds SRAM (Mobile Semiconductor SRAM compilers for the RH90 rad-hard process, BusinessWire 2022-06-09), not DRAM. So no buyer pays for this trade, which would also cost $10-20M of NRE, take 36-60 months to revenue, and need a TRL-3 capacitor module SkyWater does not have. Partner note: SkyWater has been an IonQ subsidiary since 2026-07-31; IonQ says it will keep serving foundry customers.
wins_axis: none for the named buyer: trust is not required for COTS SDRAM, and price and lifecycle are already met by COTS
buyer: DoD DMSMS offices and avionics primes
us_manufacturability: SkyWater Fab 25 (Austin TX) or Bloomington MN (DMEA Category 1A Trusted); SkyWater has been an IonQ subsidiary since 2026-07-31. U.S. OSAT packaging.
who_is_already_doing_this: Alliance, ISSI and Winbond sell commercial SDRAM at ~$2-5; Rochester does licensed re-creation. DoD's trusted-memory route at SkyWater is SRAM (RH90 SRAM compilers from Mobile Semiconductor), and rad-hard programs use SRAM/MRAM from Honeywell, BAE and Frontgrade.
fatal_flaw: No buyer at the price: COTS SDRAM is still made at $2-5 and DoDI 5200.44 trust rules target custom ICs, not commodity memory, so the market is ~$0.3-1.5M per year of gross profit against $10-20M of NRE.
possible: yes - 1T1C MIM eDRAM is production-proven elsewhere; unproven on this line
profitable: no - NRE never paid back

name: Legacy-DRAM buying cooperative for mid-size U.S. OEMs
rule1_status: PARTIAL - buyer pain SUPPORTED; supplier acceptance of a co-op LTA (no title, no credit) UNVERIFIED
wins_axis: Supply security
buyer: Mid-size OEMs buying $0.5-5M per year of legacy DRAM
us_manufacturability: None (commercial structure); can steer pooled volume to U.S.-made Manassas DDR4.
who_is_already_doing_this: Franchised distributors (Arrow, Avnet, WPG, Future), which follow makers' allocation rules. EMS turnkey procurement (contract manufacturers already pool component buying for their OEM customers). Procurement consultancies, brokers, Mobius Materials. Healthcare GPOs (Vizient, Premier) are an analogy only: no electronics GPO was found (search 2026-11-01).
fatal_flaw: Suppliers and franchised distributors may refuse an intermediary that takes neither title nor credit risk. Taking title needs $8-27M of working capital (T2). The value window is ~2027 only: allocation scarcity, the whole product, starts to ease in 2028 and is gone in a glut.
possible: marginal - hinges on one supplier honoring a pooled LTA; untested
profitable: marginal - good margins if allocation materializes

name: Memory FinOps Audit for Cloud SaaS
wins_axis: $/GiB-month of rented cloud RAM (fewer GiB-months bought)
buyer: Series A-C SaaS companies with $20k-200k/month AWS bills and no dedicated FinOps engineer
us_manufacturability: Pure software built and hosted in the U.S. (AWS us-east-1) and sold via AWS Marketplace. No fab or hardware.
who_is_already_doing_this: CAST AI, ScaleOps, StormForge (CloudBolt), Kubecost/OpenCost (IBM [UNVERIFIED-T]), PerfectScale (DoiT [UNVERIFIED-T]), Sedai, Densify, plus free tools: AWS Compute Optimizer, Robusta KRR, K8s VPA, Goldilocks. Intel closed Granulate (Tiber App-Level Optimization) in Oct-2024 after failing to find a buyer for a ~$650M acquisition (Globes, via search snippet).

The DRAM shortage never reached general EC2 list prices (only ML Capacity Blocks rose), so buyers feel no new urgency. A report-only product churns once the savings are booked, and standing read access to customer AWS accounts gates the subscription behind SOC 2 (cost and time not modeled).
possible: yes - standard FinOps mechanics, shipping at many vendors
profitable: marginal - ~$270/month ACV against free tools and funded automation vendors; churn after the savings are booked
doable_by_founder: yes - read-only AWS integration and reports; the first revenue could come from consulting in the founder's network

name: Fleet Memory-Reclaim Autopilot (TMO for on-prem)
subbranch: Transparent memory compression / proactive reclaim / dedup
wins_axis: Effective $/GB (usable GB per purchased GB), which defers DRAM capex
buyer: Regional hosting providers, MSPs running Proxmox/KVM, on-prem Kubernetes and CI/build farms, and university HPC centers that must buy DDR5 RDIMMs at 2026 prices
us_manufacturability: Pure software. Target customers' fleets sit in U.S. colos (Ashburn VA, Secaucus NJ). Builds on upstream Linux mm, Proxmox VE (KSM) and Kubernetes 1.34+.
who_is_already_doing_this: Meta (TMO/Senpai, internal), Google (zswap far memory, internal), Linux upstream (free), Red Hat/Canonical (tuned profiles), Proxmox (KSM built in). The cloud K8s optimizers (CAST AI, ScaleOps) focus on requests and instances, not swap [ESTIMATE]. MemVerge left the field.
fatal_flaw: It is configuration of free kernel features. Sophisticated operators already do it themselves, and conservative ones fear swap latency and OOM incidents. One production incident at an early customer ends the company.
possible: yes - production-proven at Meta/Google, and every component is upstream
profitable: marginal - real savings mainly for DDR5 fleets; DDR4 fleets can add used RDIMMs at ~$4-6/GB, buyers can DIY with free upstream features, and the pain halves in a glut

name: KV-Cache Tier Integration & Tuning for Self-Hosted LLMs
wins_axis: $/token and TTFT: host DRAM ($/GB) substitutes for re-computing prefill on HBM GPUs
buyer: Mid-market teams self-hosting 70B-class open models on 8-64 GPUs for data-residency reasons (legal-tech, healthcare, fintech)
us_manufacturability: Software and services. Customers' GPU clusters are in U.S. colos (Ashburn VA, NJ). Builds on Apache-2.0 LMCache, Dynamo and Mooncake.
who_is_already_doing_this: Tensormesh (the LMCache creators): $4.5M seed Oct-2025 plus a $20M extension 2026-05-27 from NVIDIA NVentures, AMD Ventures and CoreWeave; Tensormesh Inference is GA with cache-hit-rate, KV-usage and token-cost dashboards. Banking, packaging and test in the U.S. at Integra (KS), QP Technologies (CA) or Micross (Apopka FL, verified in batch 10), though Micross is also a direct competitor in authorized die.
who_is_already_doing_this: Rochester Electronics (Newburyport MA): world's largest wafer/die bank (>10B die, expansion to ~30B), described as authorized by 70+ OCMs, 15B devices and 200k part numbers in stock; legacy DRAM (SDRAM to DDR5, LPDDR4x) through an Intelligent Memory partnership and legacy NAND through SkyHigh Memory (2023). Micross (authorized die/wafer distributor, DRAM on line card, its own AS6171 lab). Intelligent Memory and Alliance Memory (long-lifecycle DRAM OCM brands). Micron Manassas long-lifecycle DDR4/LP4 via distribution since 2026-05-22. Distributors' bonded stock.
fatal_flaw: OCMs grant aftermarket authorization to proven firms with capital and quality systems. Rochester already holds >10B banked die, 70+ OCM authorizations and a legacy-DRAM partnership with Intelligent Memory, so it is the firm OCMs call first. A startup can neither win the authorization nor fund $0.6M per part ($2M+ for a portfolio). Without authorization the venture is just an independent distributor, which DFARS ranks last.
possible: yes - Rochester and Micross prove the model
profitable: yes - for incumbents with authorization and scale
doable_by_founder: no - capital, authorization and relationships are the moat

name: AS6171 counterfeit-detection and authentication lab for memory lots
wins_axis: supply security / authenticity (counterfeit-risk reduction with documentation)
buyer: AS6081 independent distributors, defense EMS and primes' purchasing departments, OEMs buying broker DRAM during the shortage
us_manufacturability: U.S. lab services; no fab.
who_is_already_doing_this: SMT Corp (Sandy Hook CT, 72,000 sq ft; ANAB ISO/IEC 17025 + AS6171 HRL2; DLA QTSL-recognized; UK lab accredited Dec 2025). Micross Clearwater FL (17025, AS6171, AS6081, ITAR; RAM tester in its electrical scope; full-lot AS6171 in ~2 weeks). A2 Global Electronics (FL/Singapore/Netherlands; AS6171/7 ATE electrical). Vyrian (Houston/Hong Kong 17025 lab, at-speed AS6171 flows). White Horse Laboratories (Cleveland; DLA-approved Qualified Commercial Test Laboratory for FSC 5961/5962). Integra Technologies and Alter Technology [UNVERIFIED-training]. Mobius Materials' ML authentication; the ERAI/GIDEP ecosystem.
fatal_flaw: Crowded, accreditation-heavy services market. SMT Corp (CT, AS6171 HRL2, DLA QTSL) is in the target corridor and Micross offers full-lot AS6171 with RAM test in ~2 weeks. Below 36 lots/month the lab loses money (-34% GM at 20). The founder cannot run it without a hired AS6171 test engineer and ~$650k; at-speed DDR5 component test equipment could push capex higher [STILL-UNVERIFIED]. Die-origin flagging uses standard AS6171 decap/die-marking methods incumbents already run, so it is not a moat.
possible: yes - routine lab methods
profitable: marginal-to-no: loses money below 36 lots/month and must take share from accredited, DLA-recognized incumbents
doable_by_founder: marginal - needs a technical hire and ~$0.65M

name: 'Compliant memory' federal reseller on GSA MAS / SEWP (compliance-as-a-product)
rule1_status: SUPPORTED for VAR mechanics; the core value claim (a compliance premium) is contradicted by FAR 25.402/25.001 and the 2026 proposed rule
kill_reason: The card's only differentiator, 'compliant memory', is something every reseller of Samsung, SK hynix, Micron or Kingston product already meets at no cost. TAA treats Korean, Taiwanese and Japanese memory as equal above $174k (FAR 25.402). The BAA component test is waived for COTS (FAR 25.001). The FAR Council's proposed rule (FAR Case 2023-008, FR 2026-03065, 2026-02-17; not final; statutory effect 2027-12-23) puts the same duty on every offeror and offers a disclosure safe harbor (law-firm alerts, via search snippet). So compliance is a feature everyone has, not a product. Against CDW-G, Carahsoft and the 2,115 SEWP VI holders (awarded Jun-2026, ordering from 2026-11-01, no on-ramp schedule found), a new entrant has no SEWP seat, no MAS track record and no volume pricing. It loses on price and access and only ties on compliance and small-business status, so it wins no axis. Whatever §5949 creates that buyers would pay for is verification (C-64), not resale margin.
wins_axis: supply security / compliance documentation
buyer: federal civilian and DoD IT buyers; prime integrators
us_manufacturability: Resale only; modules may be U.S.-assembled (Kingston, Penguin) from foreign die.
who_is_already_doing_this: 2,115 NASA SEWP VI contract holders (awarded Jun-2026, ordering from 2026-11-01; via search snippet), including many small, 8(a), SDVOSB and HUBZone VARs; CDW-G, Carahsoft and GSA MAS IT schedule holders [UNVERIFIED-training]; Micron and Kingston through their channels
fatal_flaw: No winning axis. §5949 rewards 'not Chinese', and every Samsung, SK hynix, Micron or Kingston reseller already meets it. The FAR Council's proposed rule (FAR Case 2023-008, 2026-02-17; not final; effective 2027-12-23 by statute) puts the same duty on every offeror and gives a disclosure safe harbor. TAA lets allied memory compete equally above $174k (FAR 25.402), and the BAA component test is waived for COTS (FAR 25.001). SEWP VI was awarded to 2,115 holders in Jun-2026 and is closed to a newcomer until an unscheduled on-ramp. The result is a 6-10% VAR margin with no vehicle and no price edge: $1.5-2.5M of sales per $150k of gross profit (e_estimates §7).
possible: yes - standard VAR model, but SEWP VI is closed to newcomers until an on-ramp and MAS needs a track record
profitable: no - commodity margin; compliance confers no premium
doable_by_founder: marginal - slow vehicle access, working capital ~$185-310k

name: STTR vehicle on a national-lab / university memory patent (lab-patent studio)
subbranch: University/lab patent license -> STTR -> defense Phase III
kill_reason: The card itself says C-06 (Sandia HZO FeRAM) and C-07 (Penn/AFRL AlScN license plus STTR) card the device plays, and both survived audit (batch_01, KEEP_WITH_CORRECTIONS). This vehicle options the same technologies, bids the same topics (DARPA DV017, AF254-D0806) and sells to the same buyers (AFRL/DARPA program offices, space primes). The portfolio wrapper adds no product a buyer pays for. Revenue arrives only when one of those device plays reaches Phase III, ~46 months out, and A-04 does not count grants as revenue. The Purdue In2O3 option is a TRL 3-4 research result that belongs with C-01. The one transferable insight should be folded into C-06/C-07 as their funding structure: STTR lets the lab or university PI lead while the founder keeps their day job. SBIR/STTR has been reauthorized through 2031-09-30 (S.3971, signed 2026-04-13, via search snippet), so that structure is live.
wins_axis: non-volatility plus radiation/temperature tolerance (supply security for space and hypersonics)
buyer: AFRL/DARPA program offices, space primes, hypersonic and Venus/geothermal sensor integrators
us_manufacturability: Sandia MESA (trusted, but a government fab not open for production); SkyWater S130 / Fab 25 for a commercial path. Bayh-Dole and DOE U.S.-manufacture preferences align with U.S. production.
who_is_already_doing_this: C-06 (Sandia HZO FeRAM chip) and C-07 (AlScN license plus STTR) card the device plays. Incumbents: Infineon rad-hard F-RAM, Frontgrade/Everspin Toggle MRAM. Many university spinouts run this STTR pattern.
fatal_flaw: It duplicates C-06 and C-07, and it is the grant farm the founder says they do not want. The chance of customer revenue is ~3% per topic attempt and ~15% after five (e_estimates §8). First revenue lands ~46 months out, past the 36-month ceiling. STTR also requires the small business itself to perform >=40% of the work [UNVERIFIED-training], so the vehicle needs its own technical staff or paid lab time, not just a lab PI. It depends on a PI and a fab it does not control.
possible: yes - option/STTR/Phase III mechanics are routine; device TRL 3-5
profitable: marginal - niche defense NVM can be profitable for whoever reaches Phase III, rarely within 4 years
doable_by_founder: marginal - they can run the company shell and proposals, not the science or the small business's required >=40% work share

name: SBA/search-fund acquisition of a small memory reseller at peak earnings - tempting, dangerous
rule1_status: N/A (financial structure); the value claim depends on shortage EBITDA persisting
kill_reason: On the card's own terms ($4.2M price = 3.5x $1.2M shortage EBITDA, 90% SBA 7(a) debt, ~$612k/yr debt service), DSCR is 1.96 in 2026, 0.65 in a normal year and 0.33 in the glut (e_estimates §9). The loan is repaid only if shortage pricing lasts most of a 10-year term. That makes it a leveraged, personally guaranteed long position on DRAM prices, not a venture with a product axis, and no software upside closes a 0.65 DSCR. It also fails QB-INCOMPLETE: no target is named or confirmed for sale. Under SOP 50 10 8/8.1 the 10% injection (~$420k) may draw at most half from 'limited sources' such as full-standby seller notes and <20% minority investors (via search snippet). The founder, with under $50k, would therefore need a controlling co-buyer bringing ~$210k+ cash and a guarantee. Buying the same business at trough multiples in 2028-29 would be a different, later concept.
wins_axis: time-to-revenue (acquired), not a product axis
buyer: the target's existing customers: SMB IT, refurbishers, MSPs, homelab/gaming buyers
us_manufacturability: Existing U.S. operation (testing and resale); no fab.
who_is_already_doing_this: Search funds and ETA buyers generally; ITAD consolidators such as Iron Mountain ALM (ITRenew) [UNVERIFIED-training].
fatal_flaw: Buying cyclical peak earnings with leverage. Shortage-inflated EBITDA reverts, and the SBA personal guarantee ties the founder's personal assets to the 2028 glut.
possible: yes - SBA acquisitions of small distributors are routine
profitable: no - at 2026 prices the deal cannot service its debt even in a normal year (DSCR 0.65); maybe yes if bought at trough multiples
doable_by_founder: no - equity gap (SOP 50 10 8.1 caps seller notes plus minority-investor equity at half the 10% injection) and guarantee risk

name: Acquire the 3D XPoint/Optane IP estate and license it (business-model Optane revival) - tempting, dead
kill_reason: The card concedes that IP without a line is worthless. The only XPoint line (Lehi) went to TI in 2021 for $900M cash plus ~$600M of tools and now runs analog. Micron quit, citing 'insufficient market validation' after ~$545M of underutilization charges, and Intel lost >$7B. Any product path therefore needs a new 20nm-class crosspoint PCM fab, which is >$1B (T4, A-11). The licensing-only path fails on its premise. There is no single estate to buy: the IP reportedly passed to Micron with royalty-free licenses to Intel, and an Ovshinsky bankruptcy trust sued both over title in 2020 (Blocks & Files, via snippet). A 2026 search found no revival or licensing activity. At the canonical $6.40/GB glut the cost gap that sank Optane closes again.
wins_axis: $/GB vs. DRAM plus persistence
buyer: CXL memory-tier buyers (hyperscalers, SAP HANA/database hosts)
us_manufacturability: No XPoint line exists anywhere: Lehi was sold to TI and converted to 65/45nm analog.
who_is_already_doing_this: Nobody. A 2026-11-01 search found no XPoint revival or licensing program. SanDisk's 3D-matrix/HBF work and imec selector-only-memory research are the nearest descendants (see C-25, C-53).
fatal_flaw: IP without a line is worthless, and the line is T4. No fab runs XPoint: Lehi went to TI and was converted. There is no clean estate to buy, because the IP sits with Micron with royalty-free licenses to Intel, and an Ovshinsky bankruptcy trust contested title in 2020. Micron and Intel both exited. Out-licensing memory IP takes a decade even for the best-run licensor.
possible: marginal - the technology shipped (2017-22), but there is no clean estate for sale and no line to use it on without a >$1B fab
profitable: no

name: CXL memory-tiering integration practice (consulting -> managed tuning)
kill_reason: This is the services packaging of C-49 (TB-Class CXL Node, KEEP_WITH_CORRECTIONS in batch_07). It has the same buyers (EDA, genomics, SAP HANA/in-memory DB, HPC), the same hardware (Samsung CMM-D, Micron CZ122, SK hynix CMM-DDR5) and the same tuning stack (weighted interleave, DAMON, HMSDK). Its own lens list includes 'module/appliance (VAR)', and batch_07 already flagged the overlap. The cheaper-capacity leg is C-44 (DDR4 second-life CXL expander). DDR5 CXL modules carry the same DRAM plus a controller, so they do not win on $/GB. Marvell's DDR4-reuse Structera X 3406 only samples in Q1 2027 (HPCwire 2026-10-12, via snippet). This follows the C-76/C-50 precedent, where a different packaging of the same opportunity is a duplicate. C-49 should take the assessment and managed-tuning subscription as its T0 entry path and recurring line.
wins_axis: Capacity and bandwidth per node above the native DIMM-slot ceiling, plus reuse of already-owned DDR4 once Structera-class cards reach non-hyperscaler buyers (3406 samples Q1 2027). Not $/GB for new CXL DRAM, which costs the same DRAM plus a controller.
buyer: university and DOE HPC centers, SAP HANA/in-memory database hosts, EDA and genomics shops
us_manufacturability: Services; hardware from Micron/Samsung/SK hynix/Astera/Marvell; no fab dependency.
who_is_already_doing_this: Penguin Solutions (CXL memory-expansion servers, SMART CXL AICs; per batch_07); Supermicro, Dell, HPE and Lenovo professional services; Marvell, Astera, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix field engineers (free, to sell silicon); Red Hat certified CXL hardware (CZ122); Colfax, Silicon Mechanics; MemVerge [UNVERIFIED-T for the rest]
fatal_flaw: It duplicates C-49, and demand is thin. Memory makers reportedly scaled back CXL controller development (Jul-2026). The DDR4-reuse controller for mid-market buyers only samples in Q1 2027. Vendors give integration away to sell hardware. Every billable hour is kernel or platform work the founder cannot do.
possible: yes - CXL 2.0 expanders and Linux tiering ship today
profitable: marginal - services margins, small and lumpy demand
doable_by_founder: no as a solo founder; marginal only with a kernel/CXL cofounder who delivers all billable work

name: Memory patent expiry and litigation radar
kill_reason: The card's only axis is cheaper FTO and litigation monitoring, and free tools already win it. Unified Patents' Portal offers free PTAB and district-court search plus free daily litigation alerts, and its data has been in Google Patents since 2019 (via search snippet). Google Patents and USPTO Patent Center also show status, maintenance fees and anticipated expiry free [UNVERIFIED-training]. Precision for counsel sits with Docket Navigator, Lex Machina and RPX. What the named buyers actually need, a reliable FTO opinion, must come from an attorney ($10-30k), and a dashboard cannot give legal reliance. The card's own evidence (ITC 337-TA-1487; Everspin's $6.0M litigation quarter) shows demand for counsel, not for a $4.8k/yr memory dashboard. The card calls itself 'likely a feature ... or an internal tool', consistent with the C-14 kill of a curated public-data subscription.
wins_axis: risk reduction (lower FTO and litigation-monitoring cost)
buyer: small U.S. module makers, recert/ITAD firms, CXL and memory startups, IP counsel, memory investors
us_manufacturability: Software.
who_is_already_doing_this: Unified Patents Portal (free PTAB and district-court search plus free daily litigation alerts; data integrated into Google Patents since 2019, via search snippet); Google Patents and USPTO Patent Center (free status, maintenance-fee and expiry data [UNVERIFIED-training]); Docket Navigator, Lex Machina, RPX, PatSnap, LexisNexis PatentSight (paid) [UNVERIFIED-training]
fatal_flaw: No winning axis. Litigation and PTAB monitoring is free (Unified Portal, Google Patents), expiry and maintenance status is free (USPTO, Google Patents), and the deliverable with real value, a relied-upon FTO opinion, must come from counsel. The memory-only niche (~25 subscribers x $4.8k = $120k ARR, with no demand evidence) cannot outspend free tools or entrenched paid platforms.
possible: yes
profitable: no - free tools cover monitoring, and counsel captures the FTO spend
doable_by_founder: yes - T0, but at most an internal FTO-gate tool for this study's hardware concepts, not a business
